procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Division Bench of the High Court dismissing the criminal appeal filed by the appellant (accused) and confirming his conviction and sentence awarded by the 9th Additional Sessions Judge, Vadodara in Sessions Case No. 101/2010 under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the criminal appeal filed by the appellant (accused) and confirmed his conviction and sentence. The High Court briefly narrated the facts and stated they were in complete agreement with the view taken by the Additional Sessions Judge before dismissing the appeal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (accused) appealed to the Supreme Court by way of special leave. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and remanded the case to the High Court with a request to decide the appeal afresh on merits in accordance with law, preferably within six months.

directions: The case is remanded to the High Court for deciding the criminal appeal afresh on merits.
The High Court is requested to dispose of the appeal as expeditiously as possible preferably within six months.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its appellate jurisdiction, is required to independently examine issues of fact and law, appreciate the evidence, and record reasoned findings before deciding an appeal against conviction.

facts: An accused, convicted of murder under s.302 of the Penal Code by a trial court, appealed to the High Court.
The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence.

The accused then appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court's order was flawed because it did not contain any reference to or discussion of the evidence, nor did it provide its own findings.

The Supreme Court observed that the High Court's order merely mentioned the post-mortem report, stated that "various witnesses" implicated the accused, and then deferred to the trial court's judgment, stating it was in "complete agreement" with the trial judge's "minute examination" of the evidence.
law: The Supreme Court relied on Section 386(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.), which outlines the powers of an appellate court.
The Court affirmed that a High Court, in its appellate jurisdiction, is empowered and obligated to examine issues of both fact and law when reviewing a conviction.
application: The Court held that under Section 386(b) Cr.P.C., it was "incumbent upon the High Court" to independently analyze the case.

This duty requires the appellate court to examine the evidence of each prosecution witness, consider the specific legal and factual challenges raised by the appellant, and then record its own reasoned findings.
The High Court cannot simply approve of the trial court's decision without conducting its own independent assessment.
In this specific case, the Supreme Court found that the High Court had failed in this duty by not discussing the issues, appreciating the evidence, or recording its own findings.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court is required to independently examine all issues of fact and law, appreciate the evidence, and record its own reasoned findings before deciding an appeal against conviction. Because the High Court failed to perform this duty, the Supreme Court set aside its order and remanded the matter back to the High Court for a fresh consideration on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appeal and confirming the conviction and sentence without discussing the issues, appreciating the evidence, or recording its own findings.

facts: The High Court dismissed a criminal appeal, confirming a conviction and sentence from the Additional Sessions Judge.

In its order, the High Court noted the post-mortem report, observed that the death was a homicide, and stated that evidence from "various witnesses" showed the accused was present and carried out the attack.

The High Court did not independently analyze the evidence but instead expressed "complete agreement" with the trial court, stating that the Additional Sessions Judge had "minutely examined" all the evidence and given "cogent and convincing reasons".
law: Under Section 386(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, an appellate court has the power and duty to examine both issues of fact and law.

It is incumbent upon the High Court, in its appellate jurisdiction, to examine the evidence of each prosecution witness, consider the specific challenges raised by the appellant, and record its own reasoned findings (whether of affirmation, modification, or reversal).
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to fulfill its duty as an appellate court.
Instead of independently appreciating the evidence and discussing the issues raised in the appeal, the High Court simply deferred to the trial court's findings.
The High Court's order lacked any substantive discussion of the evidence or its own findings, which is a requirement under Section 386(b) of the Cr.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the appeal in such a summary manner. The failure to independently examine the evidence and record its own findings was a procedural error. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remanded the case for a fresh decision on the merits in accordance with the law.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its appellate jurisdiction, is required to independently examine issues of fact and law, appreciate the evidence, and record reasoned findings before deciding an appeal against conviction.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that under Section 386(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the High Court, as an appellate court, has a duty to independently examine the evidence of each prosecution witness on the issues raised in the appeal.

The appellant contended that the High Court must appreciate the evidence in light of the challenges made by the accused and then record its own reasoned findings of affirmation, modification, or reversal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent likely argued that the High Court's order was sufficient, as it had concurred with the trial court's judgment which had already 'minutely examined' all the evidence and provided 'cogent and convincing reasons'.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the appeal and confirming the conviction and sentence without discussing the issues, appreciating the evidence, or recording its own findings.
appellant_arguments: The appellant argued that the High Court was not justified in dismissing the appeal because it failed to discuss any issues, appreciate the evidence, or record its own findings on the matters urged by the appellant.
The appellant contended that merely stating it was in 'complete agreement' with the trial court's view, after a brief narration of facts, does not constitute a proper disposal of a criminal appeal.
respondent_arguments: The respondent would have defended the High Court's judgment, arguing that it was justified because the High Court did peruse the record and found the trial court's reasoning to be sound, making a detailed re-appreciation of evidence unnecessary.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In its appellate jurisdiction, the High Court is empowered and obligated to examine all issues of fact and law. It must deal with the specific issues urged by the appellant, examine the evidence, and record its own findings, rather than merely expressing agreement with the lower court's judgment.
obiter: When a case is remanded for a fresh decision on its merits, the remanding court should not go into the merits of the case itself, so as to leave all issues open for the lower court to decide uninfluenced.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court failed to properly exercise its appellate jurisdiction because the Division Bench did not discuss any issues arising in the case, did not appreciate the evidence, and did not record its own findings on the matters urged by the appellant. The impugned order contained no reference to any evidence, no appreciation of it, and no discussion, which does not constitute a proper disposal of a criminal appeal.
legal_tests_applied: In view of the powers of the Appellate Court under Section 386 (b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the High Court should have examined the evidence of each prosecution witness on issues arising in the case, examined the evidence in light of the challenge made by the accused in appeal, and then recorded a finding of either affirmation, modification, or reversal.

The High Court, in its appellate jurisdiction, is empowered to examine the issues of facts and law while examining the legality and the correctness of the impugned order, and it is incumbent upon the Division Bench to deal with issues urged and then record its findings one way or the other.
